results.title: What is differential privacy in federated learning?
results.content: Differential privacy (DP) in federated learning (FL) is a technique that protects individual data privacy while allowing machine learning models to be trained across decentralized devices. In FL, data remains on users’ devices (e.g., smartphones, IoT sensors), and only model updates—not raw data—are shared with a central server. DP adds carefully calibrated noise to these updates or the aggregation process, ensuring that no single user’s data can be reverse-engineered or identified. For example, each device might add noise to its model gradients (e.g., using the Gaussian or Laplace mechanism) before sending them to the server. When the server aggregates updates from thousands of devices, the noise averages out, preserving model accuracy while obscuring individual contributions. With DP, noise ensures that unique phrases don’t disproportionately affect the global model. Developers must experiment with noise levels, aggregation frequency, and model architecture to optimize privacy-utility balance for their specific use case. results.title: Privacy by Design: Practical Challenges and Solutions in Federated Learning for Industry | by Ayush Kumar | Sep, 2025 | Medium
results.content: That combination of disciplines is what I mean by privacy-by-design, and it is what I will outline for teams trying to move federated learning, or FL, from prototype to production. Federated learning is a collaboration pattern in which many clients (mobile devices, IoT devices, hospital servers, or partner company nodes) train a model locally on their private data, and send model updates, not raw examples, to a central coordinator that aggregates them into a global model. For FL, that means threat modeling before picking algorithms, selecting privacy-enhancing technologies, and building observability and governance into every training round. 3. Engineering complexity: FL brings distributed systems challenges (client churn and unreliable connectivity), statistical issues (non-IID data), and new attack vectors (poisoning and model inversion). Regulators tend to treat FL as a privacy enhancing technology that can reduce risk, but they still expect thorough documentation, demonstrable mitigations, and DPIAs. Multinational pilots require careful legal review and clear contracts describing responsibilities, liabilities, and permitted audit rights. Defending against these attacks typically requires anomaly detection or robust aggregation, which can conflict with privacy-preserving designs if they require per-client visibility. Practical approach: use privacy accountants to track cumulative privacy loss over rounds, and choose conservative but usable epsilon budgets based on threat modeling and stakeholder risk appetite. Client layer, the SDK on devices or partner nodes, handles local training, model versioning, compression, and local clipping or noising if DP is applied on-device. Coordination layer, the server-side orchestrator, samples clients for each active round, distributes model checkpoints and hyperparameters, coordinates key exchange for secure aggregation, and handles retries for clients that drop out or fail. Federated learning can enable powerful collaborations while respecting data minimization, but privacy-by-design requires engineering discipline, cross-team coordination, and operational maturity. The right approach is layered: combine secure aggregation with differential privacy where needed, use robust aggregation to defend against active attacks, embrace personalization to address non-IID data, and invest heavily in governance, simulators, and observability. If you are about to start an FL project, begin with threat modeling and a DPIA, build simulators that represent your clients, and pick the simplest stack that satisfies your threat model.

results.title: Efficient verifiable secure aggregation protocols for federated learning - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Efficient verifiable secure aggregation protocols for federated learning. Federated learning enables collaborative model training without direct access to clients’ local data, making it highly attractive for privacy-preserving analytics in resource-constrained environments. However, existing secure aggregation protocols remain vulnerable to privacy disclosure and malicious server tampering, and often incur substantial computational and communication overhead. In this paper, we propose a verifiable secure aggregation protocol that enables efficient aggregation in resource-constrained settings while guaranteeing the integrity of the aggregated results. Second, resource-constrained edge devices incur high computational and communication overhead when running secure aggregation protocols [6]. To address these challenges, homomorphic encryption (HE) enables the server to aggregate encrypted gradients but suffers from heavy modular exponentiations and large ciphertext expansion, differential privacy (DP) injects noise to prevent inference at the cost of model utility, and secure multi-party computation (SMC) with Shamir secret sharing tolerates dropouts by reconstructing from any shares but still requires multiple communication rounds and expensive polynomial interpolations [10], [11], [12]. The use of the additive homomorphism of Shamir shares combined with a lightweight symmetric message-authentication code ensures that the server cannot manipulate the aggregated result without detection, and clients perform exactly four local operations per round—two secret-sharing operations (to distribute mask and MAC-key shares), one mask addition, and one MAC computation. We design a compute-node-assisted secure aggregation protocol that endows FL with built-in dropout robustness (tolerating up to offline clients) and allows clients to verify aggregation integrity at minimal cost. Our research contributions build upon existing work in secure aggregation within federated learning. In this study, we introduce a secure aggregation protocol for federated learning, employing computational nodes that are architecturally incapable of collective collusion and are resilient to partial dropout, as delineated in our security assumptions. ### RFLPV: A robust federated learning scheme with privacy preservation and verifiable aggregation in IoMT. ### VFL: A verifiable federated learning with privacy-preserving for big data in industrial IoT. ### LDP-FL: Practical private aggregation in federated learning with local differential privacy. ### Verifynet: Secure and verifiable federated learning. ### PriVeriFL: Privacy-preserving and aggregation-verifiable federated learning. ### Efficient verifiable protocol for privacy-preserving aggregation in federated learning.
